claims.text: Introducing a tailored self-lubricating secondary phase into CoCrFeNi will cause an in situ lubricious tribofilm to form during sliding.
The resulting tribofilm will remain stable from room temperature to 800 °C.
The tribofilm will keep both coefficient of friction and wear rate low throughout the room-temperature-to-800 °C range.
The secondary phase will react under frictional heating to create a continuous, low-shear interface.
During sliding, the secondary phase will react with oxygen or other reactive species to form a stable lubricious layer.
The lubricious layer will reduce interfacial shear forces and thereby reduce friction and wear.
Designed thermal stability of the secondary phase will maintain tribofilm formation from room temperature through high operating temperatures.
Modified CoCrFeNi will have statistically lower coefficients of friction than unmodified CoCrFeNi over the full room-temperature-to-800 °C range.
Modified CoCrFeNi will have statistically lower wear rates than unmodified CoCrFeNi over the full room-temperature-to-800 °C range.
The modified alloy will retain improved tribological performance as load and environmental conditions vary.
Improved performance is expected under sliding contact in dry air at loads typical of high-temperature tribology tests.
Performance may cease to improve if a stable tribofilm does not form at extreme temperatures or at loads beyond the tested range.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome claims robustness as environmental conditions vary, but the stated boundary and proposed experiment are restricted to dry air and do not vary the environment.

The hypothesis claims performance across the full continuous range from room temperature to 800 °C, whereas the experiment samples only room temperature, 400 °C, and 800 °C, so it cannot directly establish behavior throughout the full range.
